facts.statement: Brontomerus is a genus of camarasauromorph sauropod that lived approximately 110 million years ago during the early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Brontomerus (from Greek bronte meaning "thunder", and merós meaning "thigh") is a genus of camarasauromorph sauropod which lived during the early Cretaceous (Aptian or Albian age, approximately 110 million years ago).

facts.statement: The genus Brontomerus was named in 2011 with the type species Brontomerus mcintoshi.
facts.quote: It was named in 2011 and the type species is Brontomerus mcintoshi.

facts.statement: The specific name mcintoshi honors physicist and sauropod expert John Stanton McIntosh.
facts.quote: The specific name is in honor of physicist and North American sauropod expert John Stanton McIntosh.

facts.statement: Brontomerus is known from two fragmentary specimens representing a juvenile and an adult.
facts.quote: Brontomerus is known from two fragmentary specimens differing in size, likely a juvenile and an adult.

facts.statement: The adult Brontomerus is estimated to have weighed around six tonnes and measured approximately 14 meters in length.
facts.quote: The adult specimen is thought to have weighed around six tonnes, and probably measured around 14 meters (46 ft) in length.

facts.statement: The juvenile Brontomerus measured about 4.5 meters in length and weighed approximately 200 kilograms.
facts.quote: The juvenile specimen had about a third of this length, and probably weighed around 200 kilograms and measured 4.5 meters (15 ft) in length.

facts.statement: Brontomerus was assigned a new species status based on an oddly-shaped hipbone allowing attachment for unusually massive leg muscles.
facts.quote: Its assignment to a new species is based on several noteworthy autapomorphies, including an oddly-shaped hipbone which would have permitted the attachment of unusually massive leg muscles.

facts.statement: Brontomerus fossils were recovered from the Ruby Ranch Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in eastern Utah, United States.
facts.quote: Fossils of Brontomerus were recovered from a quarry at the top of the Ruby Ranch Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation in eastern Utah, United States.

facts.statement: The Brontomerus specimens were originally collected in 1994 and 1995 by researchers from the Sam Noble Museum.
facts.quote: The specimens were originally collected in 1994 and 1995 by a team of researchers from the Sam Noble museum of Norman, Oklahoma.

facts.statement: Brontomerus was named and described by an international team including Michael P. Taylor, Mathew J. Wedel, and Richard L. Cifelli.
facts.quote: It was named and described by Michael P. Taylor, Mathew J. Wedel and Richard L. Cifelli, an international team from the University College London, Western University of Health Sciences and the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: The fossils were found at the Hotel Mesa Quarry in easternmost Grand County, Utah.
facts.quote: The fossils were recovered from a locality known as the Hotel Mesa Quarry in easternmost Grand County, Utah.

facts.statement: The research team could not recover more complete specimens due to prior pillaging of the fossil site.
facts.quote: Due in part to this "pillaging" of the fossil site, the team was unable to recover more complete specimens.

facts.statement: In 2013, Mannion et al. classified Brontomerus as a basal somphospondyl but could not resolve its precise affinities.
facts.quote: In 2013, Mannion et al. found Brontomerus to be securely classified as a basal somphospondyl, but were not able to resolve its affinities more precisely.

facts.statement: In 2012, D'Emic considered Brontomerus a nomen dubium due to its fragmentary nature but suggested it belonged to Titanosauriformes.
facts.quote: In 2012, D'Emic concluded that Brontomerus is a nomen dubium due to the holotype's fragmentary, nondiagnostic nature, but regarded it as referrable to Titanosauriformes.

facts.statement: Brontomerus lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Dr. Michael Taylor hypothesizes that Brontomerus's strong thigh muscles were likely used for functions other than speed.
facts.quote: Dr. Michael Taylor, one of the dinosaur's describers, hypothesizes that the strong thigh muscles of Brontomerus were probably used for functions other than speed.

facts.statement: The anchoring of large femoral protraction muscles suggests Brontomerus used them to move its legs forward powerfully.
facts.quote: This is due to the apparent anchoring of large femoral protraction muscles, which would have been used to move the leg forward powerfully.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Brontomerus may have used its powerful kicks for mating competition or defense against predators like Utahraptor and Deinonychus.
facts.quote: The supposed kicks would have possibly been used for fighting over mates or in defense against predators, such as Utahraptor and Deinonychus.

facts.statement: One hypothesis is that Brontomerus's large leg muscles were used to control its unusually long legs.
facts.quote: Another possible explanation for the proportionally large leg muscles is that they were used to control unusually long legs.

rejected.quote: It is most remarkable for its unusual hipbones, which would have supported the largest thigh muscles, proportionally, of any known sauropod.
